reminder: The unit group of a ring is the group of its elements that have a multiplicative inverse.
definition: For a [ring](c:ring) $R$ with identity, the unit group $R^\times$ is the set of [invertible](c:invertible) elements, which are the $u$ with $uv=vu=1$ for some $v\in R$. With the multiplication of $R$ it is a [group](c:group), because products and inverses of units are units. It is also called the group of units.
examples: $\mathbb Z^\times=\{1,-1\}$, and for a field $k$ the unit group is $k^\times=k\setminus\{0\}$.
In $\mathbb Z[i]$ the units are $\pm1,\pm i$, so the unit group is cyclic of order $4$.
The [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) $\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]$ of the [number field](c:number-field) $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$ has the infinite unit group $\{\pm(1+\sqrt2)^n:n\in\mathbb Z\}$.
Non-example: $2$ is not a unit of $\mathbb Z$, because $2v=1$ has no integer solution, so the nonzero integers do not form a unit group.

reminder: The unit sphere about a point $x$ of a metric space is the set of points at distance $1$ from $x$.
definition: Let $(X,d)$ be a [metric space](c:metric-space) and $x\in X$. The unit sphere about $x$ is the [subset](c:subset) $S_x(X)=\{y\in X: d(x,y)=1\}$ of the points at unit [distance](c:distance) from $x$. In a [normed space](c:normed-space) with $d(y,z)=\|y-z\|$, the unit sphere about $0$ is the set of vectors of norm $1$.
examples: In $\mathbb R^2$ with the Euclidean metric, the unit sphere about $0$ is the circle $x^2+y^2=1$, and in $\mathbb R^3$ it is the surface $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$.
In $\mathbb R$, the unit sphere about $0$ is the two-point set $\{-1,1\}$.
In $\mathbb R^2$ with the metric $\max(|\Delta x|,|\Delta y|)$, the unit sphere about $0$ is the boundary of the square $[-1,1]^2$.
Non-example: the unit ball $\{y: d(x,y)\le1\}$ is not a unit sphere, because it contains $x$ itself at distance $0$.

steps: Take the sphere of radius $r$ about $x$ in $(X,d)$, which is the set $\{y: d(x,y)=r\}$.
Fix the radius $r=1$.
The set becomes $\{y: d(x,y)=1\}$, which is the unit sphere about $x$.
links.why: Facts about spheres of any radius apply to unit spheres, and in a normed space scaling turns every sphere about $0$ into the unit sphere.

steps: Take $X=\mathbb R$ with $d(y,z)=|y-z|$ and the point $x=0$.
The unit sphere is $\{y\in\mathbb R:|y|=1\}=\{-1,1\}$.
This two-point set is the [0-sphere](c:0-sphere) $S^0$.
links.why: The 0-sphere is the unit sphere of the real line, so facts about unit spheres apply to it.

steps: Take $X=\mathbb R^3$ with the Euclidean metric and the point $x=0$.
The unit sphere is the set $\{(u,v,w):u^2+v^2+w^2=1\}$.
This set is the surface of the unit ball, which is the [2-sphere](c:2-sphere).
links.why: The 2-sphere is the unit sphere of three-dimensional space, so facts about unit spheres apply to it.

reminder: A unit vector is a vector whose norm is $1$.
definition: In a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ with a [norm](c:norm) $\|\cdot\|$, a vector $v$ is a unit vector when $\|v\|=1$. Every nonzero vector $w$ gives the unit vector $w/\|w\|$, which points the same way as $w$. In an [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) the norm is $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$, so a unit vector has $\langle v,v\rangle=1$.
examples: In $\mathbb R^2$ with the Euclidean norm, $(1,0)$ and $(3/5,4/5)$ are unit vectors, and $(3,4)/5$ is the unit vector in the direction of $(3,4)$.
A state of a quantum system is a unit vector of a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space), so that the probabilities add up to $1$.
With the max norm $\max(|x|,|y|)$ on $\mathbb R^2$, the vector $(1,1)$ is a unit vector, so the answer depends on the norm.
Non-example: $(1,1)$ has Euclidean norm $\sqrt2$, and the zero vector has norm $0$, so neither is a unit vector for the Euclidean norm.

reminder: For types $A$ and $B$ in a universe, the canonical map from identifications $A=B$ to equivalences $A\simeq B$ is itself an equivalence.
definition: For types $A,B$ in a [type universe](c:type-universe) $\mathcal U$, induction on the [identity type](c:identity-type) turns each identification $p\colon A=B$ into an [equivalence of types](c:equivalence-of-types) $\mathrm{idtoeqv}(p)\colon A\simeq B$, and it sends $\mathrm{refl}_A$ to the identity. The univalence axiom says that $\mathrm{idtoeqv}\colon(A=B)\to(A\simeq B)$ is itself an equivalence for all $A,B:\mathcal U$, so equivalent types are identified. It is an added axiom of [dependent type theory](c:dependent-type-theory), not a consequence of the basic rules.
examples: By univalence, a bijection between two sets $A$ and $B$ in $\mathcal U$ gives an identification $A=B$, so isomorphic sets are equal as elements of the universe.
Univalence implies [function extensionality](c:function-extensionality), and for propositions it gives [propositional extensionality](c:propositional-extensionality).
The simplicial set model of type theory, with types as Kan complexes, satisfies the axiom.

Non-example: with [uniqueness of identity proofs](c:uniqueness-of-identity-proofs), the type $\mathbf 2=\mathbf 2$ for the two-element type $\mathbf 2$ has at most one element, but $\mathbf 2\simeq\mathbf 2$ has two (the identity and the swap), so $\mathrm{idtoeqv}$ cannot be an equivalence.

steps: Restrict $A$ and $B$ to [mere propositions](c:mere-proposition) $P$ and $Q$.
A logical equivalence $P\leftrightarrow Q$ gives an equivalence of types $P\simeq Q$, because both types are propositions.
Univalence turns this equivalence into an identification $P=Q$.
So univalence, restricted to propositions, is propositional extensionality.
links.why: It shows that propositional extensionality is the special case of univalence for propositions, so each use of univalence for propositions is a use of the weaker axiom.

reminder: A universal property characterizes an object, up to unique isomorphism, by the maps into it or out of it.
definition: A universal property says that an object $U$, together with some data such as a map or a cone, is an [initial object](c:initial-object) or a [terminal object](c:terminal-object) of the [category](c:category) of all objects with that kind of data. So every other object with such data has exactly one map to $U$, or from $U$, that respects the data. Two objects with the same universal property are [isomorphic](c:isomorphism) by a unique isomorphism that respects the data.
examples: The product $A\times B$ with projections $p_1,p_2$: each pair of maps $f\colon X\to A$ and $g\colon X\to B$ factors as $(p_1h,p_2h)$ through exactly one map $h\colon X\to A\times B$.
The free group $F(S)$ on a set $S$: every map from $S$ to a group $G$ extends to exactly one group homomorphism $F(S)\to G$.
The tensor product $V\otimes W$ of vector spaces: every bilinear map out of $V\times W$ factors through exactly one linear map out of $V\otimes W$.

Non-example: the set $P=\{0,1\}$ with both projections equal to the identity is not a product of $\{0,1\}$ with itself, because the pair of maps from a one-point set with values $0$ and $1$ does not factor through $P$.

steps: Take a category $\mathcal C$ with an [initial object](c:initial-object) $I$ and no extra data.
For each object $X$ of $\mathcal C$, there is exactly one morphism $I\to X$.
So $I$ has a universal property: its maps out of $I$ characterize it, and it is unique up to unique isomorphism.
links.why: An initial object is the simplest universal property, so every universal property is an initial or terminal object in the right category.

steps: Take a [product](c:product) $A\times B$ with projections $p_1\colon A\times B\to A$ and $p_2\colon A\times B\to B$.
The data is the pair of projections, and the competing objects are all triples $(X,f,g)$ with maps $f\colon X\to A$ and $g\colon X\to B$.
Each triple factors as $(p_1h,p_2h)$ through exactly one map $h\colon X\to A\times B$.
So $A\times B$ is a terminal object in the category of these triples.
links.why: A product is a universal property of maps into an object, so the same reasoning gives uniqueness of products up to unique isomorphism.

steps: Take the [free object](c:free-object) $F(S)$ on a set $S$, with the map $\iota\colon S\to F(S)$.
Compare it with all pairs of an object $G$ and a map $f\colon S\to G$.
Freeness says that each $f$ extends along $\iota$ to exactly one structure-preserving map $F(S)\to G$.
So $(F(S),\iota)$ is initial among these pairs, which is a universal property.
links.why: A free object is a universal property of maps out of an object, so the same reasoning gives uniqueness of free objects up to unique isomorphism.

reminder: A morphism is universally closed when every pullback of it is a closed morphism.
definition: Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a [morphism of schemes](c:morphism-of-schemes). It is universally closed when, for every morphism $Y'\to Y$, the [pullback](c:pullback) $X\times_YY'\to Y'$ is a [closed morphism](c:closed-morphism), which means that it sends closed sets to closed sets. In particular $f$ is closed, and the closedness survives every [base change](c:base-change).
examples: Every closed immersion is universally closed, because every pullback of a closed immersion is again a closed immersion.
For a field $k$, the map $\mathbb P^n_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is universally closed, which is a form of the main theorem of elimination theory.
A continuous map of topological spaces is universally closed exactly when it is closed and all its fibres are quasi-compact.

Non-example: $\mathbb A^1_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is closed but not universally closed, because its pullback along itself is the projection $\mathbb A^2_k\to\mathbb A^1_k$, which sends the closed curve $xy=1$ onto the non-closed set $\mathbb A^1_k\setminus\{0\}$.

steps: Take a universally closed morphism $f\colon X\to Y$.
Pull $f$ back along the identity of $Y$, which gives $f$ again up to isomorphism.
By definition this pullback is closed, so $f$ is a [closed morphism](c:closed-morphism).
The extra condition is that every other pullback of $f$ is closed too.
links.why: Facts about closed morphisms apply to universally closed ones, and the extra condition makes the property stable under base change.

steps: Take a proper morphism $f$ of schemes, which is separated, of finite type, and universally closed.
Forget the conditions of separatedness and finite type, and keep only the closedness of all pullbacks.
So every proper morphism of schemes is universally closed, and universal closedness is the part of properness that remains.
links.why: It shows that universal closedness is the part of properness that the valuative criterion tests.

reminder: The unknot is the knot that is isotopic to the standard round circle.
definition: A [knot](c:knot) is an [embedding](c:embedding) of a [circle](c:circle) into $\mathbb R^3$ or $S^3$. The unknot is the knot that is [isotopic](c:isotopy) to the standard round circle, such as the circle $x^2+y^2=1$ in the plane $z=0$. Equivalently, it is the knot that bounds an embedded disc.
examples: The round circle $x^2+y^2=1$ in the plane $z=0$ is the unknot.
A loop with one kink has a diagram with one crossing, but one [Reidemeister move](c:reidemeister-move) removes the crossing, so it is the unknot.
A knot that has a diagram with at most two crossings is the unknot, because every nontrivial knot needs at least three crossings.
Non-example: the [trefoil knot](c:trefoil-knot) is not the unknot, because its diagram has a $3$-colouring that uses all three colours, the unknot has none, and Reidemeister moves keep this property.

steps: Take a knot $K$, which is an embedding of a circle into $\mathbb R^3$.
Add the condition that $K$ is isotopic to the standard round circle.
A knot that satisfies this condition is the unknot, so every unknot is a knot.
links.why: General facts about knots, such as diagrams and Reidemeister moves, apply to the unknot, which is the trivial case that every knot invariant must handle.

reminder: An upper set of a poset is a subset that contains every element above each of its members.
definition: Let $P$ be a set with a [partial order](c:partial-order), or just a [preorder](c:is-preorder), written $\le$. A [subset](c:subset) $U\subseteq P$ is an upper set when $x\in U$ and $x\le y$ imply $y\in U$. Its complement is a lower set, which is a subset closed downwards.
examples: In $(\mathbb R,\le)$, the upper sets are $\varnothing$, $\mathbb R$, and the rays $[a,\infty)$ and $(a,\infty)$.
In the power set of $\{1,2,3\}$ ordered by inclusion, the sets that contain the element $1$ form an upper set.
Every union and every intersection of upper sets is an upper set.
Non-example: in $(\mathbb R,\le)$, the interval $[0,1]$ is not an upper set, because $1\in[0,1]$ and $1\le2$, but $2\notin[0,1]$.

steps: Take an element $x$ of $P$ and its [up set](c:up-set) $x{\uparrow}=\{y: x\le y\}$.
If $y\in x{\uparrow}$ and $y\le z$, then $x\le z$ by transitivity, so $z\in x{\uparrow}$.
So $x{\uparrow}$ is an upper set, and it is the smallest upper set that contains $x$.
links.why: Up sets are the simplest upper sets, and every upper set is the union of the up sets of its elements.

steps: Take a [filter](c:filter) $\mathcal F$ of a partial order $P$, for example a filter of subsets of a set.
If $x\in\mathcal F$ and $x\le y$, then $y\in\mathcal F$, because a filter is closed upwards.
So $\mathcal F$ is an upper set of $P$.
A filter adds two conditions: it is nonempty, and any two of its members have a common lower bound in $\mathcal F$.
links.why: Facts about upper sets apply to filters, which are the upper sets that are also directed downwards.

reminder: The Vandermonde determinant of $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is $\prod_{i<j}(x_j-x_i)$, the determinant of the matrix of powers $x_i^{j-1}$.
definition: For elements $x_1,\dots,x_n$ of a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring), the Vandermonde [matrix](c:matrix) is $V=(x_i^{\,j-1})_{i,j=1}^n$. Its [determinant](c:determinant) is the Vandermonde determinant $\Delta(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_{1\le i<j\le n}(x_j-x_i)$, which is a [polynomial](c:polynomial) in the $x_i$. Over a field, $\Delta\ne0$ exactly when the $x_i$ are pairwise distinct.
examples: For $n=2$, $\det\begin{pmatrix}1&x_1\\1&x_2\end{pmatrix}=x_2-x_1$.
Distinct nodes $x_1,\dots,x_n$ give $\Delta\ne0$, so exactly one polynomial of degree less than $n$ takes prescribed values at the $x_i$.
Non-example: the matrix with rows $(1,x_i,x_i^3)$ is not a Vandermonde matrix, because it skips the power $x_i^2$; its determinant is $\Delta\cdot(x_1+x_2+x_3)$, not $\Delta$.

reminder: A vector measure is a countably additive function on measurable sets with values in a topological vector space.
definition: Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) and let $M$ be a commutative [additive monoid](c:add-comm-monoid) with a topology, such as a [topological vector space](c:topological-vector-space). A vector measure is a function $\mu$ from the [measurable sets](c:measurable-set) of $X$ to $M$ with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$ such that, for pairwise disjoint measurable sets $A_n$, the [series](c:series) $\sum_n\mu(A_n)$ converges to $\mu\big(\bigcup_nA_n\big)$ in every order. In the Lean library mathlib, $\mu$ also takes the value $0$ on sets that are not measurable.
examples: Every [finite measure](c:finite-measure) and every finite [signed measure](c:signed-measure) is a vector measure with values in $\mathbb R$.
For an integrable function $f$ from $[0,1]$ to a [Banach space](c:banach-space) $E$, the map $\mu(A)=\int_Af\,d\lambda$ is a vector measure with values in $E$.
Non-example: $A\mapsto\lambda(A)^2$ on the Borel subsets of $[0,1]$ is not a vector measure, because $\lambda([0,\tfrac12))^2+\lambda([\tfrac12,1])^2=\tfrac12\ne1=\lambda([0,1])^2$.

steps: Take a [signed measure](c:signed-measure) $\mu$ with only real values on a measurable space.
Its values lie in the vector space $\mathbb R$ with its usual topology.
For disjoint sets $A_n$, countable additivity gives $\sum_n\mu(A_n)=\mu\big(\bigcup_nA_n\big)$ in every order of the terms.
So $\mu$ is a vector measure with values in $\mathbb R$.
links.why: A vector measure keeps the additivity of a signed measure and allows values in other spaces, so results on signed measures extend to vector values.

steps: Take a [finite measure](c:finite-measure) $\mu$, so $0\le\mu(A)\le\mu(X)<\infty$ for every measurable set $A$.
Then $\mu$ is a function with real values, and $\mathbb R$ is a topological vector space.
For disjoint sets $A_n$, the series $\sum_n\mu(A_n)$ has nonnegative terms and converges to $\mu\big(\bigcup_nA_n\big)$ in every order.
links.why: A finite measure is the nonnegative real-valued case of a vector measure.

reminder: A Verma module is the universal module generated by a highest weight vector of a given weight $\lambda$.
definition: Let $\mathfrak g$ be a [semisimple Lie algebra](c:is-semisimple) over an algebraically closed field $F$ of characteristic $0$, with a [Cartan subalgebra](c:cartan-subalgebra) $\mathfrak h$, a choice of positive roots, and the Borel subalgebra $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. For a [weight](c:weight) $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, let $F_\lambda$ be the one-dimensional $\mathfrak b$-module on which $\mathfrak h$ acts by $\lambda$ and $\mathfrak n^+$ acts by $0$. The Verma module is $M(\lambda)=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak b)}F_\lambda$, formed with the [universal enveloping algebra](c:universal-enveloping-algebra), and it is a [representation](c:lie-algebra-representation) of $\mathfrak g$ by left multiplication.
examples: For $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ with basis $e,h,f$, the module $M(\lambda)$ has basis $v_k=f^kv_0$ for $k\ge0$, and $h\,v_k=(\lambda-2k)v_k$.
For $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, $M(\lambda)$ is irreducible unless $\lambda=n$ is a nonnegative integer, and then it has a submodule $M(-n-2)$ with the $(n+1)$-dimensional simple module as quotient.
Every simple highest weight module of highest weight $\lambda$ is the unique simple quotient of $M(\lambda)$.
Non-example: the $2$-dimensional natural module of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ is a highest weight module but not a Verma module, because every Verma module of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ has infinite dimension.

steps: Take $M(\lambda)=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak b)}F_\lambda$, with $\mathfrak g$ acting by left multiplication on the first factor.
This action makes $M(\lambda)$ a [representation](c:lie-algebra-representation) of $\mathfrak g$.
The vector $1\otimes1$ generates $M(\lambda)$, has weight $\lambda$, and is killed by $\mathfrak n^+$.
The special case adds this highest weight vector, and $M(\lambda)$ is free of rank one over $U(\mathfrak n^-)$.
links.why: General facts about representations apply to Verma modules, and the highest weight vector adds the tools of weight theory.

reminder: The Vietoris complex of a metric space has a simplex for each finite set of points of diameter at most $\varepsilon$.
definition: For a [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, the Vietoris complex $V_\varepsilon(X)$ is the [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex) on $X$ whose [simplices](c:simplex) are the finite nonempty subsets of [diameter](c:diameter) at most $\varepsilon$. Dowker's theorem uses a variant for a [relation](c:relation) $R\subseteq X\times Y$, whose simplices are the finite nonempty subsets of $X$ that have a common $R$-partner in $Y$.
examples: For $X=\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon=1$, the complex $V_1(X)$ is an infinite path, because only neighbouring integers are within distance $1$.
For $n\ge4$ equally spaced points on a circle and $\varepsilon$ just large enough to join neighbours, $V_\varepsilon$ is an $n$-gon, which has the homotopy type of a circle.
If $X$ is finite and $\varepsilon\ge\operatorname{diam}X$, then every nonempty subset is a simplex, so $V_\varepsilon(X)$ is the full simplex on $X$.
Non-example: for $\varepsilon=1$ and the points $0,1,2$ of $\mathbb R$, the set $\{0,1,2\}$ is not a simplex of $V_1$, because its diameter is $2$, even though $\{0,1\}$ and $\{1,2\}$ are edges.

reminder: In a Vitali family, every fine cover of a set has disjoint members that cover almost all of the set.
definition: Let $X$ be a [metric space](c:metric-space) with a [measure](c:measure) $\mu$. A Vitali family assigns to each point $x$ a family $\mathcal F(x)$ of [measurable sets](c:measurable-set) with nonempty [interior](c:interior), such that for every $\varepsilon>0$ some member of $\mathcal F(x)$ lies in the closed ball of radius $\varepsilon$ about $x$. It also has the covering property: if $s\subseteq X$ and each $x\in s$ has a subfamily $\mathcal G(x)\subseteq\mathcal F(x)$ with arbitrarily small members, then some pairwise disjoint sets $A_t\in\mathcal G(x_t)$ with $x_t\in s$ cover $s$ except for a $\mu$-[null set](c:null-set).
examples: In $\mathbb R^n$ with Lebesgue measure, the closed balls $\bar B(x,r)$ with $r>0$ form a Vitali family, which is the Vitali covering theorem.
In a second countable metric space with the [Besicovitch covering property](c:has-besicovitch-covering), the closed balls about each point form a Vitali family for every locally finite measure.
More generally, for a uniformly locally doubling measure on a metric space, the closed balls about each point form a Vitali family.
Non-example: in $\mathbb R$ with Lebesgue measure, let $\mathcal F(x)=\{\{x\}\}$. A singleton has empty interior, so this is not a Vitali family.

reminder: The von Neumann hierarchy has $V_0=\varnothing$, $V_{\alpha+1}=\mathcal P(V_\alpha)$, and $V_\lambda=\bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda}V_\alpha$ at limit stages.
definition: By transfinite recursion on the [ordinals](c:ordinal), put $V_0=\varnothing$ (the [empty set](c:empty-set)), $V_{\alpha+1}=\mathcal P(V_\alpha)$ (the [power set](c:power-set)), and $V_\lambda=\bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda}V_\alpha$ for limit ordinals $\lambda$. The stages increase, and under the [axiom of foundation](c:axiom-of-foundation) every set lies in some $V_\alpha$. The least such $\alpha$ is the [rank](c:rank-of-a-set) of the set.
examples: $V_0=\varnothing$, $V_1=\{\varnothing\}$, $V_2=\{\varnothing,\{\varnothing\}\}$, and $V_3$ has $4$ elements.
The stage $V_\omega=\bigcup_nV_n$ is the set of [hereditarily finite sets](c:hereditarily-finite-set), and it is countable.
The set $\omega=\mathbb N$ first appears in $V_{\omega+1}$, because its rank is $\omega$.
Non-example: the sequence $S_0=\varnothing$, $S_{n+1}=S_n\cup\{S_n\}$ is not the hierarchy, because it gives only the von Neumann ordinals $0,1,2,\dots$, which are some of the elements of $V_\omega$.

steps: Run the recursion only up to the first limit ordinal $\omega$.
Each $V_n$ with $n<\omega$ is finite, because $V_0$ is empty and the power set of a finite set is finite.
A set lies in $V_\omega$ exactly when its transitive closure is finite, which means that it is hereditarily finite.
So the hereditarily finite sets form the stage $V_\omega$ of the hierarchy.
links.why: The hereditarily finite sets are the first infinite stage of the hierarchy, so general facts about the hierarchy apply to them.

reminder: The wave trace of a compact Riemannian manifold is the distribution $\sigma(t)=\sum_je^{-it\lambda_j}$, where $\lambda_j^2$ are the Laplacian eigenvalues.
definition: Let $M$ be a [compact](c:compact-space) [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) without boundary, and let $\lambda_j^2$, with $\lambda_j\ge0$, be the [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue) of its [Laplace-Beltrami operator](c:laplace-beltrami-operator), counted with multiplicity. The wave trace is the trace of the wave group $e^{-it\sqrt\Delta}$, which is $\sigma(t)=\sum_je^{-it\lambda_j}$, and this sum converges as a [distribution](c:distribution) on $\mathbb R$. The Duistermaat-Guillemin trace formula says that its singularities lie at $0$ and at the lengths of the [closed geodesics](c:closed-geodesic) of $M$, and at their negatives.
examples: On the circle $\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$, the eigenvalues are $n^2$ for $n\in\mathbb Z$, so $\sigma(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}e^{-it|n|}$, which is singular exactly at $t\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, the lengths of closed geodesics.
On the flat torus $\mathbb R^2/2\pi\mathbb Z^2$, $\lambda=|k|$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^2$, and $\sigma(t)=\sum_ke^{-it|k|}$ has its singular support inside $\{2\pi|m|:m\in\mathbb Z^2\}$ and its negatives.
Non-example: the heat trace $\sum_je^{-t\lambda_j^2}$ is not the wave trace, because it is a smooth function of $t>0$ and has no singularities at the lengths of closed geodesics.

reminder: A subset of a Banach space is weakly compact when it is compact in the weak topology.
definition: Let $X$ be a [normed space](c:normed-space), for example a [Banach space](c:banach-space). A subset $K\subseteq X$ is weakly compact when it is [compact](c:compact-space) in the [weak topology](c:weak-topology), which means that every cover of $K$ by weakly open sets has a finite subcover. It is relatively weakly compact when its weak closure is weakly compact. By the Eberlein-Smulian theorem, in a Banach space this means that every sequence in $K$ has a subsequence that converges weakly to a point of $K$.
examples: Every norm compact subset of a normed space is weakly compact, because the weak topology is coarser than the norm topology.
The closed unit ball of a reflexive Banach space, such as $\ell^2$ or $L^p$ with $1<p<\infty$, is weakly compact.
In $\ell^2$, the set $\{e_n:n\ge1\}\cup\{0\}$ is weakly compact, because $e_n\to0$ weakly.
Non-example: the closed unit ball of $c_0$ is not weakly compact, because $c_0$ is not reflexive.

steps: Take a normed space $X$ and give it the [weak topology](c:weak-topology).
A subset $K$ is [compact](c:compact-space) in this topology when every cover of $K$ by weakly open sets has a finite subcover.
This is weak compactness, so it is compactness for a chosen coarse topology.
links.why: Facts about compact sets apply to weakly compact sets, and the coarse topology makes weak compactness hold in many more sets than norm compactness.

reminder: A subset of a dual space is weak-* compact when it is compact in the weak-* topology.
definition: Let $X$ be a [normed space](c:normed-space) with [dual space](c:dual-space) $X^*$. A subset $K\subseteq X^*$ is weak-* compact when it is [compact](c:compact-space) for the [weak-star topology](c:weak-star-topology), which is the coarsest topology that makes every evaluation $\varphi\mapsto\varphi(x)$ with $x\in X$ continuous. A weak-* closed and norm bounded subset of $X^*$ is weak-* compact, and for a Banach space $X$ the converse holds.
examples: By the Banach-Alaoglu theorem, every closed ball of $X^*$ is weak-* compact.
The set of probability measures on a compact metric space $K$ is weak-* compact in $C(K)^*$, because it is weak-* closed and lies in the closed unit ball.
The closed unit ball of $\ell^\infty=(\ell^1)^*$ is weak-* compact, although it is not norm compact.
Non-example: the whole dual $X^*$ of an infinite-dimensional Banach space $X$ is not weak-* compact, because every weak-* compact set is norm bounded.

steps: Take a normed space $X$ and give its dual $X^*$ the [weak-star topology](c:weak-star-topology).
A subset $K\subseteq X^*$ is [compact](c:compact-space) in this topology when every cover by weak-* open sets has a finite subcover.
This is weak-* compactness, so it is compactness for a chosen coarse topology on a dual space.
links.why: Facts about compact sets apply to weak-* compact sets, for example that a weak-* compact set is closed in the Hausdorff weak-* topology.

steps: Take a subset $K$ of a dual space $X^*$ that is [weakly compact](c:weak-compactness), for the topology $\sigma(X^*,X^{**})$.
The weak-* topology $\sigma(X^*,X)$ is coarser, because $X$ embeds in $X^{**}$ by evaluation.
A cover of $K$ by weak-* open sets is a cover by weakly open sets, so it has a finite subcover.
So $K$ is weak-* compact, and the two notions agree when $X$ is reflexive.
links.why: A weakly compact subset of a dual space is weak-* compact, so a weak compactness proof also gives weak-* compactness there.

reminder: A weak derivative $v=\partial_iu$ satisfies $\int u\,\partial_i\varphi=-\int v\,\varphi$ for every smooth compactly supported $\varphi$.
definition: Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be an [open set](c:open-set) and let $u$ be [integrable](c:integrable-function) on every compact subset of $\Omega$. A function $v$ with the same property is the weak derivative $\partial_iu$ when $\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx=-\int_\Omega v\,\varphi\,dx$ for every [test function](c:test-function) $\varphi$ on $\Omega$, with the [integrals](c:lebesgue-integral) taken for Lebesgue measure. It is unique up to a null set, and it agrees with the classical [partial derivative](c:partial-derivative) when $u$ is $C^1$.
examples: For $u(x)=|x|$ on $(-1,1)$, the weak derivative is $\operatorname{sgn}(x)$, although $u$ has no classical derivative at $0$.
Every $C^1$ function has its classical partial derivatives as weak derivatives, by integration by parts.
A function of the [Sobolev space](c:sobolev-space) $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is an $L^p$ function whose weak first derivatives lie in $L^p$.

Non-example: the Heaviside function $H=\mathbf 1_{[0,\infty)}$ has no weak derivative, because its distributional derivative is the [Dirac distribution](c:dirac-distribution) $\delta_0$, which is not a locally integrable function.

steps: Take $u\in C^1(\Omega)$ and a [test function](c:test-function) $\varphi$ on $\Omega$.
Integration by parts gives $\int u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx=-\int(\partial_iu)\,\varphi\,dx$, because $\varphi$ vanishes near the boundary.
So the classical partial derivative $\partial_iu$ satisfies the defining identity of a weak derivative.
The weak derivative keeps this identity as its definition, so it also covers functions such as $|x|$.
links.why: The weak derivative extends differentiation to functions that are not differentiable everywhere, and it agrees with the classical derivative where both exist.

steps: Regard a locally integrable function $u$ as the distribution $\varphi\mapsto\int u\,\varphi\,dx$.
The [derivative of the distribution](c:derivative-of-a-distribution) is $\varphi\mapsto-\int u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx$, by definition.
This distribution comes from a function $v$ exactly when $\int u\,\partial_i\varphi=-\int v\,\varphi$ for all test functions.
In that case $v$ is the weak derivative, so the special case adds that the distributional derivative is a function.
links.why: Facts about derivatives of distributions apply to weak derivatives, which are the ones that stay functions.

reminder: A weight space is the set of vectors $v$ with $x\cdot v=\lambda(x)v$ for all $x$ in the Lie algebra.
definition: Let $V$ be a [representation](c:lie-algebra-representation) of a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak g$ over a field $F$, and let $\lambda\colon\mathfrak g\to F$ be a linear form. The weight space is $V_\lambda=\{v\in V: x\cdot v=\lambda(x)\,v\text{ for all }x\in\mathfrak g\}$, a subspace of $V$, and $\lambda$ is a [weight](c:weight) of $V$ when $V_\lambda\ne0$. In the theory of semisimple Lie algebras, a [Cartan subalgebra](c:cartan-subalgebra) $\mathfrak h$ takes the place of $\mathfrak g$.
examples: Let $\mathfrak h$ be the diagonal matrices in $\mathfrak{gl}_n(F)$ acting on $F^n$. For $\varepsilon_i(\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\dots,a_n))=a_i$, the weight space $V_{\varepsilon_i}$ is the line spanned by the basis vector $e_i$.
By Lie's theorem, a nonzero finite-dimensional representation of a solvable Lie algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$ has a weight $\lambda$ with $V_\lambda\ne0$.

Non-example: for the diagonal $\mathfrak h\subset\mathfrak{gl}_2$ acting on $F^2$, the vector $e_1+e_2$ lies in no weight space, because $\operatorname{diag}(a,b)$ sends it to $ae_1+be_2$, which is not a multiple of it when $a\ne b$.

steps: Take a one-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak g=Fx$ acting on $V$ through the linear map $T=x\cdot{}$.
A linear form $\lambda$ on $\mathfrak g$ is determined by the scalar $\lambda(x)$.
Then $v\in V_\lambda$ means $Tv=\lambda(x)v$, because the condition for $x$ gives the condition for every multiple of $x$.
So $V_\lambda$ is the [eigenspace](c:eigenspace) of $T$ for the eigenvalue $\lambda(x)$.
links.why: A weight space is an eigenspace for a whole Lie algebra of operators at once, so eigenspace facts extend to commuting families and Lie algebras.

reminder: A weighted sum of numbers $x_i$ with weights $w_i$ is $\sum_iw_ix_i$.
definition: Let $I$ be a finite index set, let $x_i$ be [real numbers](c:real-number) and let $w_i$ be real weights, usually nonnegative. The weighted sum is the [finite sum](c:finite-sum) $\sum_{i\in I}w_ix_i$. With all $w_i=1$ it is the plain sum, and with $\sum_iw_i=1$ it is a [weighted mean](c:weighted-mean).
examples: A course grade with weight $0.3$ on an exam score $80$ and weight $0.7$ on a project score $90$ is the weighted sum $0.3\cdot80+0.7\cdot90=87$.
The [expected value](c:expected-value) of a finite random variable is the weighted sum $\sum_ip_ix_i$, with the probabilities $p_i$ as weights.
The weighted Hölder inequality bounds a weighted sum: $\sum_iw_if_i\le\big(\sum_iw_i\big)^{1-1/p}\big(\sum_iw_if_i^p\big)^{1/p}$ for nonnegative $w_i,f_i$ and $p\ge1$.
Non-example: the weighted product $\prod_ix_i^{w_i}$ multiplies the terms instead of adding them, so it is not a weighted sum.

steps: Take the vector space $\mathbb R$ over the field $\mathbb R$ and the vectors $x_1,\dots,x_n$.
Use the weights $w_i$ as the scalar coefficients.
Then $\sum_iw_ix_i$ is the [linear combination](c:linear-combination) of the $x_i$ with these coefficients.
links.why: A weighted sum follows the algebra of linear combinations, so it is linear in the weights and in the values.

steps: Take a [weighted mean](c:weighted-mean) of the $x_i$ with weights $w_i\ge0$ that add up to $W>0$.
Divide each weight by $W$ to get $c_i=w_i/W$, with $\sum_ic_i=1$.
The weighted mean is then the weighted sum $\sum_ic_ix_i$ with the weights $c_i$.
links.why: A weighted mean is a weighted sum with weights that add up to $1$, so weighted sum estimates apply to means.

reminder: The Whitehead torsion of a homotopy equivalence of finite complexes is an element of $\mathrm{Wh}(\pi_1)$ that vanishes exactly for simple homotopy equivalences.
definition: Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a [homotopy equivalence](c:homotopy-equivalence) of finite [CW complexes](c:cw-complex) and let $\pi=\pi_1(Y)$. The mapping cone of the lift of $f$ to the universal covers gives a finite acyclic based [chain complex](c:chain-complex) of free modules over the [group ring](c:group-ring) $\mathbb Z[\pi]$, and its torsion in [K-theory](c:algebraic-k-theory) is an element of $K_1(\mathbb Z[\pi])$. The Whitehead torsion $\tau(f)$ is its class in the Whitehead group $\mathrm{Wh}(\pi)=K_1(\mathbb Z[\pi])/\{\pm g:g\in\pi\}$.
examples: The identity map and the inclusion of a subcomplex into a complex that collapses onto it have $\tau=0$.
$\mathrm{Wh}(\pi)=0$ for $\pi$ trivial, $\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb Z^n$, so every homotopy equivalence of finite complexes with such a fundamental group has torsion $0$.
The lens spaces $L(7,1)$ and $L(7,2)$ are homotopy equivalent, but no homotopy equivalence between them has torsion $0$, so they are not simple homotopy equivalent.

Non-example: the inclusion $S^1\hookrightarrow D^2$ has no Whitehead torsion, because it is not a homotopy equivalence and its mapping cone chain complex is not acyclic. For an [h-cobordism](c:h-cobordism) $(W;M,M')$, the torsion is that of the inclusion $M\hookrightarrow W$.

reminder: The length $|w|$ of a word $w$ is the number of letters in it, counting repeats.
definition: A [word](c:word) over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a finite sequence $w=a_1a_2\cdots a_n$ of letters $a_i\in\alpha$, and its length is $|w|=n$, so the empty word has length $0$. In a [group](c:group) with a [generating set](c:generating-set) $S$, the word length of an element $g$ is the least length of a word in $S\cup S^{-1}$ that equals $g$.
examples: The word $abba$ over $\{a,b\}$ has length $4$, and the empty word has length $0$.
In a [prefix code](c:prefix-code) over an alphabet of $D$ letters, the word lengths of the codewords satisfy Kraft's inequality $\sum_wD^{-|w|}\le1$.
In $\mathbb Z$ with the generating set $\{1\}$, the element $-3$ has word length $3$, and in the free group on $a,b$ the element $aba^{-1}$ has word length $3$.
Non-example: the number of distinct letters is not the length, because $abab$ uses two letters but has length $4$.

reminder: A Yang-Mills instanton is a connection on a $4$-manifold whose curvature satisfies $\star F=\pm F$.
definition: Let $P\to M$ be a [principal bundle](c:principal-bundle) with structure group $SU(n)$ over an oriented [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $M$ of dimension $4$, such as a closed manifold or $\mathbb R^4$. An instanton is a [connection](c:principal-connection) $A$ on $P$ whose [curvature](c:curvature-form) is self-dual or anti-self-dual, $\star F_A=\pm F_A$, where $\star$ is the [Hodge star](c:hodge-star). On a closed $M$, such a connection minimizes the Yang-Mills energy $\int_M|F_A|^2$ among connections on $P$, the minimum is a fixed multiple of $|c_2(P)|$, and many authors also require $c_2(P)\ne0$ to exclude flat connections.
examples: The [BPST instanton](c:bpst-instanton) is an anti-self-dual $SU(2)$ connection over $S^4$ whose second Chern number has absolute value $1$.
For $SU(2)$ on $S^4$, the moduli space of instantons with $|c_2|=k\ge1$ has dimension $8k-3$.
A flat connection has $F=0$, so $\star F=\pm F$ holds, but it has $c_2=0$, and many authors do not call it an instanton.

Non-example: on the trivial $SU(2)$ bundle over $\mathbb R^4$, the connection $A=\mathrm{diag}(i,-i)\,x_1\,dx_2$ has $F=\mathrm{diag}(i,-i)\,dx_1\wedge dx_2$ and $\star F=\mathrm{diag}(i,-i)\,dx_3\wedge dx_4\ne\pm F$, so it is not an instanton.

steps: Take an instanton $A$ with $\star F_A=\pm F_A$ on an oriented $4$-manifold.
Apply $d_A$ to get $d_A\star F_A=\pm d_AF_A$.
The Bianchi identity gives $d_AF_A=0$.
So $d_A\star F_A=0$, which is the Yang-Mills equation, and the instanton adds the first-order condition $\star F=\pm F$.
links.why: General results on Yang-Mills connections apply to instantons, which are the Yang-Mills connections with a first-order equation.

steps: Take a gauge field of $SU(n)$ Yang-Mills theory, which is a connection on a principal bundle.
A nonzero second Chern class puts the connection in a nontrivial topological sector, away from the trivial configurations.
The Yang-Mills instanton adds that the curvature is self-dual or anti-self-dual, so it minimizes the energy in its sector.
links.why: It places the Yang-Mills instanton inside the general idea of an instanton, which is a gauge field in a nontrivial topological sector.

steps: Take the [BPST instanton](c:bpst-instanton), an $SU(2)$ connection on $\mathbb R^4$ that extends over $S^4$.
Its curvature is anti-self-dual, so $\star F=-F$.
Its energy is finite and its second Chern number has absolute value $1$.
So it is a Yang-Mills instanton of charge one.
links.why: The BPST instanton is the basic example of a Yang-Mills instanton, so general instanton facts apply to it.

reminder: The zero section of a vector bundle sends each point of the base to the zero vector of the fibre over it.
definition: Let $\pi\colon E\to X$ be a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle). Its zero section is the [section](c:section) $s_0\colon X\to E$ that sends each $x\in X$ to the zero vector $0_x$ of the fibre $E_x$, so that $\pi\circ s_0=\mathrm{id}_X$. It embeds $X$ in $E$ as the set of zero vectors, and every vector bundle has it.
examples: For the trivial bundle $X\times\mathbb R^n$, the zero section is $x\mapsto(x,0)$.
For the tangent bundle $TM$ of a smooth manifold, the zero section is the zero vector field, and $M$ sits in $TM$ as its zero section.
In the normal bundle of a submanifold $X\subseteq M$, a tubular neighbourhood sends the zero section to $X$.
Non-example: in $X\times\mathbb R^n$, the map $x\mapsto(x,v)$ with $v\ne0$ is a section but not the zero section, because its values are not zero vectors.

steps: Take a vector bundle $\pi\colon E\to X$ and a point $x\in X$.
The fibre $E_x$ is a vector space, so it has a zero vector $0_x$.
Define $s_0(x)=0_x$, so that $\pi\circ s_0=\mathrm{id}_X$ and $s_0$ is a [section](c:section) of $\pi$.
The special case adds that the value at each point is the zero vector of the fibre.
links.why: General facts about sections apply to the zero section, which is the base point of the vector space of all sections.

reminder: In a zero-sum game, the payoffs of all players add up to zero for every outcome.
definition: A game is zero-sum when, for every choice of strategies, the payoffs of all players add up to $0$. A finite two-player zero-sum game is therefore given by one [matrix](c:matrix) $A=(a_{ij})$ of [real numbers](c:real-number): player 1 picks a row $i$, player 2 picks a column $j$, player 1 receives $a_{ij}$, and player 2 receives $-a_{ij}$.
examples: In matching pennies the payoff matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}$, so player 1 wins $1$ when the coins match and loses $1$ otherwise.
Rock-paper-scissors with payoff $1$ for a win, $-1$ for a loss and $0$ for a tie is a zero-sum game, and its optimal play uses [mixed strategies](c:mixed-strategy).
Chess with score $+1$ for a win, $-1$ for a loss and $0$ for each player in a draw is a zero-sum game.
Non-example: in the prisoner's dilemma with payoffs $(3,3)$, $(0,5)$, $(5,0)$ and $(1,1)$, the sums are $6$, $5$ and $2$, so it is not zero-sum.
